From 2016 to 2018, the amount of cocoa beans produced rose from 1.63 to 2.11 million metric tons, a slightly greater proportional increase than the area harvested showed over the same years.
From 2010 to 2020, the area harvested nearly doubled, from 2.28 to 4.27 million hectares, while the amount of cocoa beans produced grew by a smaller proportion.

table.title: Cocoa Bean Production and Area Harvested in Côte d’Ivoire, 2010–2020
columns: Cocoa beans produced (millions of metric tons)

items.explanation: Yield is the amount harvested per hectare, so it rises only when output grows faster than the land harvested. The table shows the reverse: from 2010 to 2020 the area harvested grew from 2.28 to 4.27 million hectares (about 87 percent), while production grew from 1.30 to 2.20 million metric tons (about 69 percent). Output per hectare therefore fell slightly, so the extra cocoa came from additional land, as the student concludes.

A.recipe: IRREL: levels in one year instead of changes
A.why_wrong: These figures for 2020 are accurate, but values from a single year cannot show whether the growth since 2010 came from more land or from higher yields.

B.recipe: PART: accurate but insufficient (both measures rose)
B.why_wrong: It is true that both measures rose, but that is consistent with yields rising too; it does not show that output grew no faster than the land harvested.

C.recipe: CONTRA / wrong window: accurate reading of one interval that points the other way
C.why_wrong: This is accurate (about 29 percent against about 28 percent), but it covers only 2016 to 2018, and output growing faster than land in that interval means yield rose slightly then, which points away from the student’s conclusion rather than supporting it.

sources.what: FAO cocoa bean production for Côte d’Ivoire by year (1.30 million t in 2010, 2.20 million t in 2020)
FAO cocoa bean yields for Côte d’Ivoire (0.571 t/ha in 2010, 0.516 t/ha in 2020); area harvested in the table = production divided by yield

items.notes: Band-7 moves: proxy (yield = output per hectare, stated only in the passage, must be applied to two columns that do not show yield); key is a contrast in rates; B is an accurate but insufficient reading (both rose), A is levels instead of changes, C is an accurate 2016 to 2018 reading that points the other way (reviewer replaced a reversed-proportion mirror of the key). Operations: read 2010 and 2020 in both columns, compute two proportional changes, compare, apply the relation. All option statements checked in Python.

fixes: replaced C (reversed-proportion mirror of key D, killed by the same 2010 to 2020 computation) with an accurate 2016 to 2018 reading that points the other way (production +29%, area +28%, checked on unrounded FAO values)
review.notes: Area = production / yield matches the FAO/OWID CSVs for every year.

band7.why: after the C fix: yield proxy stated only in the passage, key is a contrast in rates, A levels, B both-rose, C an accurate wrong-window reading pointing against the conclusion; four reads, two ratios, a comparison

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a causal conclusion (treated vs comparison schools, right outcome)
items.passage: In the early 2000s, government schools throughout rural India replaced a monthly distribution of free grain, which pupils carried home to their families, with a free cooked lunch served at school every day. Because a meal served on school premises benefits only the children who are present to eat it, the change could influence daily attendance as well as overall enrollment. Comparing schools in one rural area that had already introduced cooked meals with schools still distributing grain, economist Farzana Afridi concluded that the meals improved daily attendance in the lowest grades.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Afridi’s conclusion?
options: Many families in the area reported that the monthly grain ration their children brought home had usually been shared among all members of the household.
The number of children enrolled in the area’s schools was about the same after the switch to cooked meals as it had been before the switch.
After the switch, the share of enrolled first graders present on a typical school day rose more in schools serving cooked meals than in schools still distributing grain.
Both before and after the switch, attendance rates among children in the upper grades were higher than attendance rates among children in the lower grades.
items.explanation: Afridi concluded that cooked meals improved daily attendance in the lowest grades. A finding that the share of first graders present on a typical day rose more in schools that served meals than in schools that still gave out grain measures exactly that outcome, in the right grades, against the right comparison, so it supports her conclusion.

A.recipe: OFF: how the grain ration was used
A.why_wrong: How families shared the grain ration says nothing about whether cooked meals changed attendance.

B.recipe: OFF: enrollment, not attendance
B.why_wrong: Unchanged enrollment concerns how many children were signed up, not how many came to school each day, which is what the conclusion is about.

D.recipe: TRAP: comparison across grades, not across kinds of schools
D.why_wrong: A gap between upper and lower grades that existed before and after the switch does not show that the meals changed attendance in the lower grades.

sources.what: Afridi, The Impact of School Meals on School Participation: Evidence from Rural India (ISI Delhi DP 10-02, 2010; J. Development Studies 2011): transition from monthly free grain to daily cooked meals; difference-in-differences with school panel data; significant improvement in daily participation in lower grades (grade 1 girls' attendance more than 12 points higher); no significant effect on enrollment

items.notes: Medium: one-step operationalization with the right comparison group; B is the outcome the study found unchanged (enrollment), so it neither supports nor contradicts the attendance conclusion; D compares the wrong groups.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (observance from duty, without feeling); translated novel
items.passage: Niels Lyhne is an 1880 novel by J.P. Jacobsen, translated from the Danish by Hanna Astrup Larsen in 1919. In the novel, Jacobsen characterizes the family of the title character’s mother as observing religious customs from a sense of obligation rather than from any genuine religious feeling: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Niels Lyhne most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “The Blid family were practical folk who accepted things as they were; they did their work, slept their sleep, and never thought of demanding any diversions beyond the harvest home and three or four Christmas parties.”
“They never passed through any religious experiences, but they would no more have dreamed of not rendering unto God what was God’s than they would have neglected to pay their taxes.”
“[T]heir natures had nothing of the poetic; beauty never stirred any raptures in them, and they were never visited by vague longings or day-dreams.”
“[T]hey said their evening prayers, went to church at Easter and Whitsun, sang their hymns on Christmas Eve, and partook of the Lord’s Supper twice a year.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: the family keeps up religious customs, and they do so from duty rather than deep feeling. Choice B says they “never passed through any religious experiences” (no deep feeling) yet would no more fail to render “unto God what was God’s” than fail to “pay their taxes,” comparing their religion to a routine obligation. Only this quotation shows both parts.

A.recipe: LURE / OFF: practical character, keyword (Christmas)
A.why_wrong: This shows the family's plain, practical habits and mentions Christmas parties, but it says nothing about why or how they observe religious customs.

C.recipe: HALF: absence of feeling, but about beauty
C.why_wrong: This shows that the family lacked strong feelings, but about beauty and poetry, not about religion, and it says nothing about duty.

D.why_wrong: This lists the religious customs the family kept, but on its own it does not show that they kept them from duty rather than deep feeling.

sources.what: J. P. Jacobsen, Niels Lyhne (1880), trans. Hanna Astrup Larsen (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1919), Project Gutenberg #55389, chapter I; quotations copied verbatim (C begins mid-sentence and D drops an opening 'Therefore', both marked with a bracketed capital)

items.notes: Medium two-part claim; key is the only option that joins observance to its motive; D is the observance half (its opening 'Therefore' is bracketed out so it does not point to an unseen reason), C is the feeling half on the wrong object, A a keyword lure. Work not used in any official item or in the bank (grep Jacobsen, Lyhne).

fixes: added translation year "in 1919" (copyright page of the Gutenberg text), as CB gives one
review.notes: All four quotations verbatim against Gutenberg #55389, chapter I; bracketed capitals mark mid-sentence starts.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (seeks approval, meets disapproval); translated comic novel
items.passage: St. Peter’s Umbrella is an 1895 novel by Kálmán Mikszáth, translated from the Hungarian by B.W. Worswick in 1900. In the novel, Mikszáth characterizes Pál Gregorics as perpetually seeking the approval of his fellow townspeople yet receiving nothing but their disapproval: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from St. Peter’s Umbrella most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Nature had blessed Pál Gregorics with a freckly face and red hair, which made people quote the old saying, ‘Red-haired people are never good.’”
“So Pál Gregorics made up his mind to prove that it was untrue. All these old sayings are like pots in which generations have been cooking for ages, and Pál Gregorics intended to break one of them.”
“He had beautiful bouquets sent from Vienna for Mrs. Vozáry, and one fine evening he let five hundred nightingales loose in Mrs. Muskulyi’s garden.”
“Pál Gregorics was always chasing Popularity, and instead of finding it came face to face with Criticism, a much less pleasing figure.”
items.explanation: The claim pairs Gregorics's constant pursuit of approval with the disapproval he receives instead. Choice D says he “was always chasing Popularity” (seeking approval) and “instead of finding it came face to face with Criticism” (receiving disapproval), so it is the only quotation that shows both parts.

A.recipe: HALF: disapproval only
A.why_wrong: People quote an unkind saying about red-haired men, which shows a prejudice against Gregorics, but nothing here shows him seeking anyone's approval.

B.recipe: HALF: effort only
B.why_wrong: Gregorics resolves to disprove an old saying, which shows his effort to be thought well of, but the quotation does not show the town disapproving of him.

C.recipe: HALF / LURE: lavish efforts to please, no response shown
C.why_wrong: His gifts of bouquets and nightingales show him trying to please particular women, not the town as a whole, and the quotation does not say how anyone responded.

sources.what: Kálmán Mikszáth, St. Peter's Umbrella (1895), trans. B. W. Worswick (Jarrold & Sons, 1900; Harper 1901), Project Gutenberg #31945, Part II, chapter I; quotations copied verbatim (inner quotation marks in A set as single quotes)

items.notes: Medium two-part claim; three half-matches (disapproval only, effort only, effort toward a different audience with no response). The sentence 'And he was as good a man as you could wish to see ... induce people to misunderstand his intentions' was left out because it also carries both parts. Work not used in any official item or in the bank (grep Mikszáth, Umbrella).

review.notes: All four quotations verbatim against Gutenberg #31945; A sets inner quotes as single quotes.

items.subtype: Data completion: pairwise comparison of two groups on the measure the claim names
items.passage: Since 2019, the polling company YouGov has periodically asked about 2,000 adults in Great Britain to classify their diets, offering categories such as meat eater, flexitarian (someone who eats mostly vegetarian food but occasionally consumes meat or fish), vegetarian, and vegan. In the January 2022 survey, the youngest respondents were the most likely to avoid meat entirely: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: 10% of respondents aged 18–24 described themselves as vegetarian, compared with only 3% of respondents aged 65 and older.
20% of respondents aged 18–24 described themselves as flexitarian, compared with only 13% of respondents aged 65 and older.
5% of respondents aged 25–49 described themselves as vegetarian, the same percentage as among respondents aged 50–64.
3% of respondents aged 50–64 described themselves as vegan, compared with only 2% of respondents aged 25–49.

table.title: Self-Reported Diets of Adults in Great Britain by Age Group, January 2022 (percentage of respondents)
table.note: Rows do not add up to 100 because some respondents chose other categories.

items.explanation: The example must show the youngest respondents more often avoiding meat entirely, which vegetarians and vegans do. Choice A does this: 10% of respondents aged 18–24 were vegetarian, compared with 3% of those aged 65 and older.

B.recipe: IRREL: true, wrong measure (flexitarians still eat some meat)
B.why_wrong: These figures are accurate, but flexitarians occasionally eat meat or fish, so they do not avoid meat entirely.

C.recipe: IRREL: sameness, and not the youngest group
C.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it compares two middle age groups that did not differ, so it does not show the youngest respondents avoiding meat more often.

D.recipe: CONTRA: true data pointing the other way
D.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it shows an older group slightly more likely to be vegan than a younger one, the opposite of the pattern the example illustrates.

sources.what: YouGov 'Dietary choices of Brits' tracker via OWID, survey of 4 January 2022, about 2,000 adults: meat eater / flexitarian / vegetarian / vegan (%) 18-24: 52/20/10/5; 25-49: 68/16/5/2; 50-64: 73/14/5/3; 65+: 78/13/3/0; pescetarian and 'none of these' omitted

items.notes: Medium pairwise completion: the passage's definition of flexitarian is what rules out B; C and D are accurate but either show no difference or the reverse direction. Pescetarian and 'none of these' columns omitted (hence the table note).

review.notes: All cells match the OWID YouGov CSV (4 January 2022).

items.subtype: Data completion: treated vs control at the same site
items.passage: Like other legumes, chickpeas can obtain nitrogen with the help of rhizobia, soil bacteria that live in nodules on the plants’ roots. Because the soils at their study sites contained few rhizobia compatible with chickpeas, researchers led by Endalkachew Wolde-meskel tested whether coating seeds with the bacteria, a practice called inoculation, could raise yields on smallholder farms in Ethiopia. Inoculated plots generally outproduced uninoculated control plots on the same farms: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the example?
options: in 2014 at Damote, control plots yielded about 2,000 kilograms of chickpeas per hectare, more than control plots at any other location shown.
in 2015 at Ginir, inoculated plots yielded less than 1,200 kilograms of chickpeas per hectare, the lowest yield of any inoculated plots shown.
in 2015 at Gimbichu, inoculated plots yielded about 2,400 kilograms of chickpeas per hectare, whereas control plots yielded only about 1,500.
in 2014 at Adaa, control plots yielded about 2,300 kilograms of chickpeas per hectare, whereas inoculated plots yielded about 1,900.

figure.title: Average Chickpea Yields on Inoculated and Control Plots at Four Year/Location Combinations in Ethiopia
figure.description: Grouped bar graph with two bars for each year and location (control plots, inoculated plots); y-axis 0 to 3,000 in steps of 500. 2014, Adaa: control about 1,940, inoculated about 2,270. 2014, Damote: control about 2,010, inoculated about 2,560. 2015, Gimbichu: control about 1,510, inoculated about 2,410. 2015, Ginir: control about 960, inoculated about 1,170. Inoculated plots are higher than control plots at every location.

items.explanation: The example must show inoculated plots outproducing control plots. In 2015 at Gimbichu, inoculated plots yielded about 2,400 kilograms per hectare and control plots only about 1,500, so choice C completes the example.

A.recipe: IRREL: control plots only, compared across sites
A.why_wrong: This is true, but it compares control plots at different locations and says nothing about how inoculated plots did.

B.recipe: PART: inoculated plots only, no control
B.why_wrong: This is true, but it gives only the inoculated yield at Ginir; without the control yield it cannot show inoculated plots outproducing control plots.

D.recipe: INACC: values swapped between the two bars
D.why_wrong: At Adaa in 2014, inoculated plots yielded about 2,300 kilograms per hectare and control plots about 1,900, not the reverse.

sources.what: Wolde-meskel et al. 2018, Agriculture, Ecosystems and Environment 261: 144-152 (open access, PMC5946702): on-farm trials in Ethiopia 2012-2015 with control and inoculated plots on the same farms; few or no compatible rhizobia in soils; Table 4 yields (kg/ha) control vs inoculated: 2014 Adaa 1937 vs 2272; 2014 Damote 2006 vs 2560; 2015 Gimbichu 1510 vs 2413; 2015 Ginir 958 vs 1170

items.notes: Medium P5 completion: key pairs the treated and control bars at one site; A compares controls across sites, B gives one bar only, D swaps the two bars. Values are the paper's Table 4 means; the P and P+I treatments are left out.

review.notes: Values match Table 4 of the paper.

items.subtype: Data description: two-part claim across two dates (behind, then far ahead)
items.passage: The printing press, introduced in Europe in the mid-fifteenth century, made books dramatically cheaper, but readers in different countries did not adopt them at the same pace. Economic historians Eltjo Buringh and Jan Luiten van Zanden estimated the number of books consumed annually per person in European countries between 1475 and 1775. Examining their estimates, a student concludes that the Netherlands and Great Britain, which lagged behind Italy in book consumption during the sixteenth century, had moved far ahead of it by the late seventeenth century.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: Book consumption per 1,000 people in the Netherlands increased from 1575 to 1625 and again from 1625 to 1675, and consumption in Spain also increased over both of those periods.
In 1575, Italy consumed more books per 1,000 people than either the Netherlands or Great Britain did, but in 1675 each of those countries consumed more than three times as many as Italy did.
In 1675, Great Britain consumed fewer books per 1,000 people than the Netherlands did but more books per 1,000 people than either Italy or Spain did in that year.
In 1575, Italy consumed more books per 1,000 people than Spain did, and in 1675 Italy’s consumption was about four times that of Spain.

table.title: Estimated Annual Book Consumption in Four European Countries, 1575–1675 (books per 1,000 people)

items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: the Netherlands and Great Britain trailed Italy in the sixteenth century, and they were far ahead of it by the late seventeenth century. Choice B shows both: in 1575 Italy (51) was ahead of the Netherlands (34) and Great Britain (27), and in 1675 the Netherlands (259) and Great Britain (192) each consumed more than three times as many books per 1,000 people as Italy (56).

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate changes without the comparison to Italy
A.why_wrong: This is true, but it never compares the Netherlands with Italy and says nothing about Great Britain, so it cannot show those countries moving ahead of Italy.

C.why_wrong: This is true of 1675, but it says nothing about the sixteenth century, when the conclusion says Great Britain lagged behind Italy.

D.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of the wrong pair (Italy and Spain)
D.why_wrong: This is true, but the conclusion concerns the Netherlands and Great Britain, not Spain.

sources.what: Buringh and van Zanden (2009), Journal of Economic History, annual per capita book consumption by country 1475-1775 (OWID grapher): Italy 0.0510/0.0421/0.0563, Netherlands 0.0335/0.1390/0.2594, Great Britain 0.0273/0.0800/0.1918, Spain 0.0043/0.0088/0.0143 books per person in 1575/1625/1675 (shown per 1,000 people, rounded); in 1525 Italy 0.0213, Netherlands 0.0142, Great Britain 0.0146

items.notes: Medium two-part claim (behind, then far ahead); A, C and D are accurate statements that miss one part or the right pair. Per-person values converted to books per 1,000 people and rounded. 'Lagged during the sixteenth century' holds for 1525 and 1575 in the source.

review.notes: All cells match the OWID Buringh and van Zanden CSV after conversion.

items.subtype: Data completion: lookup of one named cell
items.passage: The Rwenzori Mountains, which straddle the international border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo, consist of six massifs separated by deep gorges. In 1906, an Italian expedition led by the Duke of the Abruzzi reached the highest summits in the range and named several of them after European explorers and royalty. A student researching the expedition notes that the highest point of Mount Speke is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: 5,109 meters.
4,843 meters.
4,798 meters.
4,890 meters.

table.title: Highest Points of Five Massifs in the Rwenzori Mountains

items.explanation: The statement asks for the highest point of Mount Speke. According to the table, Mount Speke's highest point is 4,890 meters.

A.recipe: WGRP: neighboring row (Mount Stanley)
A.why_wrong: 5,109 meters is the highest point of Mount Stanley, not Mount Speke.

B.recipe: WGRP: neighboring row (Mount Baker)
B.why_wrong: 4,843 meters is the highest point of Mount Baker, not Mount Speke.

C.why_wrong: 4,798 meters is the highest point of Mount Emin, not Mount Speke.

sources.what: Rwenzori: six massifs separated by deep gorges; Stanley 5,109 m, Speke 4,890 m, Baker 4,843 m, Emin 4,798 m, Gessi 4,715 m; Duke of the Abruzzi's 1906 expedition scaled the highest peaks and named several

items.notes: Easy one-cell lookup with value-only options; distractors are the values of other rows.

items.subtype: Data completion: filter rows by a categorical column
items.passage: The Seychelles, an island nation in the western Indian Ocean, consists of 115 islands. Most are low coral islands, but several dozen are granitic: they are composed of granite, fragments of an ancient continental landmass, and many of them rise dramatically from the surrounding ocean. A student preparing a geography report finds that two examples of granitic islands are ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Mahé and Silhouette.
Praslin and Coëtivy.
Silhouette and Assumption.
Assumption and Coëtivy.

table.title: Five Islands of the Seychelles

items.explanation: The statement needs two islands that are granitic. The table lists Mahé and Silhouette as granitic, so choice A completes the statement.

B.recipe: WGRP: one row of the wrong type
B.why_wrong: Praslin is granitic, but Coëtivy is a coral island.

C.recipe: WGRP: one row of the wrong type
C.why_wrong: Silhouette is granitic, but Assumption is a coral island.

D.recipe: WGRP: both rows of the wrong type
D.why_wrong: Assumption and Coëtivy are both coral islands.

sources.what: List of islands of Seychelles: Mahé 155.01 km2, 905 m, Granitic; Praslin 38.00 km2, 367 m, Granitic; Silhouette 20.10 km2, 751 m, Granitic; Assumption 11.60 km2, 32 m, Outer Islands (Aldabra Group, coral); Coëtivy 9.33 km2, 21 m, Southern Coral Group; 115 islands

items.notes: Easy filter (CB 1.12 shape): exactly one option names two granitic islands. Areas rounded to one decimal.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim about influence (one-step operationalization)
items.passage: Warli painting, an artistic tradition of the Warli people of western India, was traditionally practiced by women, who decorated the mud walls of their homes with white figures to celebrate weddings, festivals, and harvests. In the 1970s, Warli artist Jivya Soma Mashe began painting every day rather than only for rituals, working on paper and canvas instead of walls. A student claims that Mashe’s work introduced Warli painting to audiences far beyond the villages where it originated.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the student’s claim?
options: Warli painters traditionally made their white paint by mixing rice flour with water and adding gum to help it stick.
Within a few years of Mashe’s first paintings on paper, his work was exhibited in France, and it later appeared in a major exhibition in Paris.
Mashe’s two sons both learned to paint in the Warli style and became well-known Warli artists themselves.
Many Warli paintings show scenes from daily life, such as farming, fishing, and people dancing in a circle.
items.explanation: The student claims that Mashe's work brought Warli painting to audiences far from the Warli villages. If his paintings were exhibited in France within a few years and later in a major Paris exhibition, people far from western India saw them, which directly supports the claim.

A.recipe: OFF: how the paint was made
A.why_wrong: How the traditional white paint was made says nothing about who saw Mashe's work.

C.recipe: OFF / SUBJ: the art passed on within the family
C.why_wrong: That his sons became Warli artists shows the art continuing in his family, not reaching audiences far beyond the villages.

D.why_wrong: What Warli paintings depict says nothing about how far Mashe's work traveled.

sources.what: Jivya Soma Mashe (1934-2018): in the 1970s began painting Warli works on an everyday basis rather than for rituals, on paper and canvas; first exhibition outside India at the Palais de Menton, France, in 1976; later shown internationally (Magiciens de la terre, Centre Pompidou, Paris); two sons are well-known Warli artists. Warli painting: done on mud walls with white pigment of rice flour and water with gum, traditionally by women, for weddings, festivals and harvests

items.notes: Easy: the key states the claim's outcome (audiences far from the villages) directly; the three distractors are accurate facts about Warli painting and Mashe that miss it.

items.subtype: Quotation from a historian supports a student's claim about an artist
items.passage: Agnes Pelton (1881–1961) painted portraits and landscapes early in her career, but she is best known today for her abstract paintings, which reflected her spiritual beliefs. In late 1931, she settled in Cathedral City, a small town in the California desert, intending only a short stay; she remained there for nearly thirty years. In a paper, an art history student claims that the desert setting where Pelton spent her later years shaped the imagery of her abstract paintings.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by an art historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “Pelton was born in Stuttgart, Germany, to American parents, and because of poor health she was taught at home for much of her childhood.”
“Two of Pelton’s early paintings were shown at the 1913 Armory Show in New York, an exhibition that introduced many Americans to modern art.”
“In 1938, Pelton became one of the founding members of the Transcendental Painting Group, a circle of artists in New Mexico who promoted abstract painting.”
“Once Pelton moved to the desert, its brilliant light and wide skies began to appear in her abstract paintings as glowing horizons and bands of color.”
items.explanation: The student claims that Pelton's desert surroundings shaped the imagery of her abstract paintings. Choice D says that after her move to Cathedral City, the desert's light and skies appeared in those paintings as glowing horizons and bands of color, which directly supports the claim.

A.recipe: OFF: biographical detail from her childhood
A.why_wrong: Her birthplace and schooling say nothing about how the desert affected her abstract paintings.

B.recipe: OFF: early career, wrong time
B.why_wrong: The 1913 exhibition of her early paintings came long before she moved to the desert, so it does not show the desert's influence.

C.recipe: OFF / LURE: abstract art, but no link to the desert
C.why_wrong: Joining a group of abstract painters concerns her abstract work, but the quotation does not connect that work to the desert setting.

sources.what: Agnes Pelton (1881-1961): born in Stuttgart to American parents, educated at home due to poor health; two paintings in the 1913 Armory Show; settled in Cathedral City, California, in late 1931, intending a visit, and lived there nearly 30 years, writing of the desert's light and skies; member of the Transcendental Painting Group; abstract art reflecting spiritual beliefs

items.notes: Easy: the key names the claim's two elements (desert setting, imagery of the abstractions); the three distractors are accurate facts about Pelton that miss the claim. Quotations are invented and unattributed; every fact inside them matches the source (the key's reading of her imagery follows her own words about the desert's light and skies and the 2019 to 2020 exhibition title Desert Transcendentalist).

items.subtype: Data completion: two comparisons of the same pair (2x2 factorial options)
items.passage: Martinique and Dominica are neighboring islands in the Lesser Antilles, an arc of islands in the eastern Caribbean Sea. Both were formed by volcanic activity, and both have rugged, mountainous interiors covered in tropical rainforest. Consulting the table, a geography student notes that in comparison with Dominica, Martinique has ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: a larger area and a higher highest point.
a smaller area and a higher highest point.
a larger area and a lower highest point.
a smaller area and a lower highest point.

table.title: Area and Highest Point of Two Islands in the Lesser Antilles

items.explanation: According to the table, Martinique's area (1,128 square kilometers) is larger than Dominica's (750 square kilometers), but its highest point (1,397 meters) is lower than Dominica's (1,447 meters). Choice C states both comparisons correctly.

A.recipe: WDIR: second comparison reversed
A.why_wrong: Martinique's area is larger, but its highest point is lower than Dominica's, not higher.

B.recipe: WDIR: both comparisons reversed
B.why_wrong: Martinique has a larger area and a lower highest point, the reverse of both comparisons here.

D.why_wrong: Martinique's highest point is lower, but its area is larger than Dominica's, not smaller.

sources.what: Martinique: area 1,128 km2, highest point Mont Pelée 1,397 m; Dominica: area 750 km2, highest point Morne Diablotins 1,447 m
Dominica area 750 km2; Morne Diablotins 1,447 m

items.notes: Easy 2x2 factorial (CB 1.3 shape); the key is the mixed combination, so neither 'both larger' nor 'both smaller' works.

items.subtype: Data description: group comparison (one category against the other) supports a conclusion
items.passage: Astronomers classify the moons of Jupiter into two broad categories. Regular moons, such as Io and Ganymede, probably formed from a disk of gas and dust encircling the young planet; they travel in nearly circular orbits that lie close to the plane of Jupiter’s equator. Irregular moons, such as Himalia and Pasiphae, are generally considered to be asteroids that Jupiter’s gravity captured much later, and they are small and follow stretched, tilted orbits. Comparing data on five of these moons, an astronomy student concludes that irregular moons typically orbit at much greater distances from Jupiter than regular moons do.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the student’s conclusion?
options: Both regular moons orbit less than 1.1 million kilometers from Jupiter, while each of the three irregular moons orbits more than 11 million kilometers away.
Ganymede, which has the largest diameter of any moon in the table, orbits more than twice as far from Jupiter as Io does.
Io and Ganymede each have a diameter of more than 3,000 kilometers, which is larger than the diameter of any of the irregular moons in the table.
Pasiphae, an irregular moon, has a diameter of about 58 kilometers and orbits farther from Jupiter than any other moon in the table does.

table.title: Diameter and Average Orbital Distance of Five Moons of Jupiter

items.explanation: The conclusion compares the two categories on distance from Jupiter. Choice A does exactly that: both regular moons orbit within about 1.1 million kilometers, while all three irregular moons orbit more than 11 million kilometers away.

B.recipe: IRREL: comparison within one category
B.why_wrong: This compares two regular moons with each other, so it says nothing about how irregular moons differ from regular ones.

C.why_wrong: This compares the categories by diameter, not by distance from Jupiter, which is what the conclusion is about.

D.recipe: PART: a single moon, no comparison with the regular moons
D.why_wrong: This describes only one irregular moon; it does not compare irregular moons as a group with regular moons.

sources.what: Moons of Jupiter (table from JPL data): Io 3,642.6 km, 421,700 km; Ganymede 5,268.2 km, 1,070,400 km; Himalia 139.6 km, 11,439,000 km; Ananke 29.1 km, 21,029,500 km; Pasiphae 57.8 km, 23,463,200 km; regular moons (prograde, nearly circular, low-inclination orbits) formed in the circumplanetary disk; irregular moons small, on eccentric, inclined orbits, irregular moons thought to be captured asteroids

items.notes: Easy group comparison (CB 1.22 shape): only A compares the two categories on the measure the conclusion names; B is within-category, C the wrong measure, D one moon only. Diameters rounded to whole kilometers.

review.notes: Pasiphae distance 23,463,200 km is the Moons of Jupiter list value (its own page gives about 24.1 million); either way it is the farthest, so no option changes.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (individual versus species-level choice; the comparison group must be other birds of the same species)
items.passage: Many birds that nest on open ground, such as nightjars and plovers, depend on camouflage rather than concealment: their eggs, and in some species the incubating adult, blend in with the surrounding soil and leaf litter. Within a single species, however, individuals can differ considerably in the color and markings of their eggs and plumage. Studying nine such species in Zambia, Martin Stevens, Jolyon Troscianko, and colleagues photographed nests with cameras calibrated to approximate the vision of predators and concluded that individual birds select nest sites suited to their own particular appearance rather than simply nesting on any ground of the shade typical for their species.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: The eggs of each species matched the ground typical of that species’ nesting areas more closely than they matched the ground where the other species nested.
Nests with eggs that closely matched the surrounding ground were less likely to be discovered by predators than were nests with poorly matched eggs.
Birds whose eggs were unusually dark for their species nested on ground that was, on average, no darker than the ground chosen by birds whose eggs were unusually pale.
A bird’s eggs generally matched the ground at its own nest more closely than they matched the ground at nests chosen by other birds of the same species.
items.explanation: The researchers conclude that each bird picks a spot suited to its own eggs and plumage, not just ground of the color its species usually nests on. To show that, a bird’s eggs must fit its own chosen spot better than they fit the spots chosen by other members of its species, which is what choice D describes. Comparing only species with species, as choice A does, would fit the view the researchers reject.

A.recipe: TRAP: fits the rejected view (species-level match)
A.why_wrong: A match between each species and its typical ground is what birds would show if they simply nested on ground of their species’ usual shade, so it does not show that individuals choose by their own appearance.

B.recipe: OFF: benefit of camouflage, not the choice of site
B.why_wrong: This shows that good camouflage protects nests, but it says nothing about whether individual birds choose sites to suit their own coloring.

C.why_wrong: If birds with dark eggs and birds with pale eggs chose equally dark ground, individuals would not be matching sites to their own appearance, which weakens the conclusion.

sources.what: Stevens, Troscianko, Wilson-Aggarwal and Spottiswoode 2017, Nature Ecology and Evolution, 'Improvement of individual camouflage through background choice in ground-nesting birds': nine species of nightjars, plovers and coursers in Zambia; vision modelling; individuals chose backgrounds that enhanced their own egg (and nightjar plumage) camouflage

items.notes: Band 6: the claim is an individual-level one, so the key needs the within-species comparison (own nest against other birds' nests). A is the species-level TRAP that fits the rejected view, B the camouflage-works OFF, C the OPP. The key matches the study's real result.

band7.why: Target 6 met: the key needs the right comparison group (other birds of the same species), two steps; A is a species-level TRAP, C the opposite, B a true-but-different question.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a causal claim about mechanism (the key supplies the missing premise: only children of working age were affected)
items.passage: In the early twentieth century, cotton cultivation in the US South depended heavily on children’s labor, and many children were kept out of school during the planting and harvesting seasons. In the years after 1915, the boll weevil, a beetle whose larvae feed on cotton buds, spread across Georgia, devastating cotton production in county after county. Economist Richard Baker found that as cotton output declined, school enrollment rose among Black children in rural Georgia, whose families disproportionately worked as tenant farmers and sharecroppers on cotton land. Baker argues that the infestation raised enrollment by making children’s work in the cotton fields less valuable to their families.
items.stem: Which finding from Baker’s research, if true, would most directly support his argument about how the boll weevil affected school enrollment?
options: In most counties, enrollment among Black children began to rise only after the boll weevil had arrived there, not in the years before its arrival.
The rise in enrollment was concentrated among children of the ages at which they had done the most fieldwork, with little change among children too young for such work.
After the boll weevil arrived, many counties used newly available state funds to open additional schools for Black children in rural areas.
Farmers in counties reached by the boll weevil spent far more on poisons such as calcium arsenate than did farmers in counties that the beetle had not yet reached.
items.explanation: Baker argues that the weevil raised enrollment because children’s work in the cotton fields became less valuable to their families. If that is the reason, the change should appear among children old enough to have been working in the fields and not among children too young to work, since their labor was never at stake. Choice B describes exactly that pattern, so it supports the specific route Baker proposes.

A.recipe: TRAP: consistent with every explanation (timing only)
A.why_wrong: A rise that follows the weevil’s arrival shows that the infestation mattered, but any effect of the crop’s collapse would produce the same timing, so it does not show that the cause was the lower value of children’s work.

C.why_wrong: New schools would be a different route to higher enrollment, so this finding points to an explanation other than the one Baker gives.

D.why_wrong: Spending on poisons describes how farmers fought the beetle; it says nothing about why children enrolled in school.

sources.what: Richard B. Baker 2015, Journal of Economic History, 'From the Field to the Classroom: The Boll Weevil's Impact on Education in Rural Georgia': boll weevil as instrument for cotton output; falling cotton output raised Black enrollment with little effect on white enrollment; cotton described as child-labor intensive

items.notes: Band-7 moves: stem names the study and the claimant (21 words); the key supplies an unstated premise (children too young to work were never part of the labor channel), turning an age contrast into evidence for the mechanism. A TRAP (timing fits every channel), C OPP (school supply), D OFF. Three steps. Age detail is hypothetical, as the stem allows; the core finding and argument are Baker's. Reviewer: the argument sentence now matches the paper’s own framing (cotton as a child-labor-intensive crop) and no longer says Baker rules out every other channel.

fixes: passage and explanation: Baker’s argument restated as the abstract frames it (falling cotton made children’s field work less valuable); dropped “not through some other consequence of the crop’s collapse”, which the source does not state (Cambridge abstract)

band7.why: Passage 106 words, stem 21 words naming Baker; the key supplies an unstated premise (only children old enough to work had labor at stake), three steps; A is a TRAP (timing fits every channel), C the rival channel, D OFF.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates between two explanations (fewer severe freezes versus higher average temperature)
items.passage: Mangroves, salt-tolerant trees that are typically killed by hard freezes, have been spreading north into salt marshes along Florida’s Atlantic coast. Analyzing satellite images taken each summer from 1984 to 2011, Kyle Cavanaugh and colleagues found that mangrove area roughly doubled near the northern limit of the trees’ range. Researchers have offered two explanations for the expansion: a gradual rise in the region’s average temperatures, or a decline in the frequency of severe cold snaps, when temperatures fall below about −4°C. Cavanaugh and colleagues concluded that the second explanation better accounts for the mangroves’ spread.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Cavanaugh and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: Mangrove area increased most at sites where severe freezes had become less frequent, including sites where average annual temperature showed no upward trend.
Mangrove area expanded more rapidly during the 2000s than during the 1980s, a period over which Florida’s climate became noticeably warmer in several respects.
In experiments, mangrove seedlings exposed to temperatures below −4°C survived about as often as seedlings that were kept above freezing.
As mangroves spread into the salt marshes, they shaded out marsh grasses and altered the habitat available to wading birds and crabs.
items.explanation: The researchers conclude that mangroves spread because severe cold snaps became rarer, not because average temperatures rose. Choice A ties the growth to fewer severe freezes even at sites where average temperature did not rise, so the expansion there cannot be credited to the rival explanation. That makes A the finding that most directly supports the conclusion.

B.recipe: TRAP: consistent with both explanations
B.why_wrong: A warming climate brings both higher averages and fewer cold snaps, so faster spread during a warmer period does not show which of the two changes drove it.

C.why_wrong: If seedlings survived severe cold as well as mild conditions, fewer cold snaps would matter little, which weakens rather than supports the conclusion.

D.recipe: OFF: effect of the expansion, not its cause
D.why_wrong: This describes what the mangroves did to the marshes, not why they were able to spread.

sources.what: Cavanaugh et al., PNAS (online Dec. 2013, print 2014), 'Poleward expansion of mangroves is a threshold response to decreased frequency of extreme cold events': Landsat 1984-2011, mangrove area doubled at the northern range limit on Florida's east coast; expansion tracked fewer days below -4 C and was uncorrelated with mean annual temperature

items.notes: Band 6 compete item. The key separates the two explanations (growth with fewer freezes where averages did not rise); B fits both, C is an OPP from a different angle (seedling cold tolerance) so the options do not mirror, D OFF.

band7.why: Target 6 met: warming predicts gains tracking mean temperature, fewer freezes predicts gains where freezes fell; the key splits them, B fits both, C the opposite route, D OFF. Short generic stem keeps it at 6.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates between a climatic and a human cause (the key supplies a rainfall measure that removes the rival)
items.passage: About 2,600 years ago, much of the rainforest of western Central Africa gave way to grassland and scattered trees, a shift recorded in pollen preserved in lake sediments throughout the region; the forest returned several centuries later. Researchers have generally attributed this “rainforest crisis” to a change toward a drier, more seasonal climate. Yannick Garcin and colleagues, however, argue that the forest was opened up mainly by people, noting that the crisis coincided with the spread of communities that farmed and smelted iron, activities that require clearing land and burning wood. To test their view, the team analyzed molecules from plant waxes preserved in the sediments of Lake Barombi in Cameroon.
items.stem: Which finding from Garcin and colleagues’ analysis of the Lake Barombi sediments, if true, would most directly support their argument?
options: The waxes indicate that grasses replaced much of the forest around the lake abruptly about 2,600 years ago, as pollen records from other lakes in the region suggest.
The waxes indicate that the plants growing around the lake in recent centuries are much like those that grew there before the crisis began.
Hydrogen isotopes in the waxes, which vary with the amount of rainfall, show no notable change during the centuries when grassland replaced the forest.
Sediment layers laid down during the crisis indicate that the level of the lake fell well below its earlier level as the forest retreated from its shores.
items.explanation: Garcin and colleagues argue that people, not a drier climate, opened up the forest. If a measure of rainfall stayed steady while grassland replaced the forest, the change in vegetation happened without the drying that the climate explanation requires, which leaves human activity as the better explanation. Choice C reports that finding, so it most directly supports their argument.

A.recipe: TRAP: consistent with both explanations
A.why_wrong: Both sides agree that grassland abruptly replaced forest about 2,600 years ago; confirming that change at Lake Barombi does not show what caused it.

B.recipe: TRAP: irrelevant property of the same record
B.why_wrong: The text already says the forest returned, and its return is expected under either explanation, so similar plants before and after the crisis do not favor one cause.

D.why_wrong: A falling lake level points to less rainfall, which supports the climate explanation the researchers argue against.

sources.what: Garcin et al. 2018, PNAS 115: 3261-3266, 'Early anthropogenic impact on Western Central African rainforests 2,600 y ago': Lake Barombi, Cameroon, plant-wax carbon and hydrogen isotopes; abrupt C4 (grass) expansion at about 2,600 cal yr BP with no simultaneous hydrological change; authors attribute the crisis to human activity (farming, iron metallurgy) rather than climate

items.notes: Band-7 moves: stem names the study and narrows the finding (21 words); passage 113 words; the key supplies the unstated premise that hydrogen isotopes record rainfall, so a vegetation change without a rainfall change removes the rival. Two TRAPs (A fits both views, B an irrelevant property), D OPP (lake level fell). The key matches the study's real result.

band7.why: Passage 111 words, stem names the study; the key needs the premise that a vegetation shift with no rainfall change removes the climate rival; A fits both views (TRAP), D fits the rival (OPP), B an irrelevant property of the same record.

items.subtype: Data description: passage number combined with the display (remittances relative to economy size)
items.passage: Remittances—funds that emigrants working abroad transfer to relatives in their home countries—constitute a substantial source of household income in many developing economies. Economists typically gauge a country’s dependence on remittances by comparing the amount it receives with the size of its economy, as measured by gross domestic product (GDP). In 2019, India’s GDP, approximately $2.8 trillion, was roughly 83 times as large as Nepal’s, approximately $34 billion. Examining World Bank data, an economics student concluded that although India received considerably more money in remittances than Nepal did that year, remittances were a substantially more important component of Nepal’s economy than of India’s.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: India received more than twice as much money in remittances as Mexico did, and more than any other country shown in the graph.
India received about $83 billion in remittances, only about ten times the roughly $8 billion that Nepal received.
Nepal received less money in remittances than Egypt, the Philippines, or Mexico did, receiving under $10 billion in total.
Nepal received roughly one-fourth as much money in remittances as India did, or a little more than $20 billion.

figure.title: Remittances Received by Five Countries, 2019
figure.description: Five bars; y-axis 0 to 90 in steps of 10. India about 83; Mexico about 40; the Philippines about 35; Egypt about 27; Nepal about 8.

items.explanation: The text says India’s economy was about 83 times as large as Nepal’s. The graph shows that India received only about ten times as much in remittances as Nepal did (about $83 billion against about $8 billion). If India’s economy is 83 times larger but its remittances only ten times larger, remittances make up a far bigger share of Nepal’s economy, roughly eight times India’s share, which is what the student concluded. Choice B describes those data.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of the wrong cells
A.why_wrong: This is accurate, but India’s large total says nothing about how important remittances are to its economy compared with Nepal’s.

C.why_wrong: This is accurate, but it gives only Nepal’s total and says nothing about India’s, so it cannot show how remittances compare in the two countries relative to the size of each economy.

D.why_wrong: The graph shows Nepal receiving about $8 billion, about one-tenth of India’s total, not one-fourth or more than $20 billion.

sources.what: World Bank World Development Indicators via API, 2019: personal remittances received (BX.TRF.PWKR.CD.DT) India 83.3 bn, Mexico 39.8 bn, Philippines 35.2 bn, Egypt 26.8 bn, Nepal 8.2 bn US dollars; GDP (NY.GDP.MKTP.CD) India 2,835.6 bn, Nepal 34.2 bn (ratio 82.9); remittances share of GDP Nepal 24.1%, India 2.9%

items.notes: Band-7 moves: the display must be read through a passage relation (share of GDP; India's economy 83 times Nepal's, given only in the text), like the holding-force/weight model 3.16. Operations: read India and Nepal, take the ratio (about 10), compare with 83, infer the share. A and C are accurate readings of the wrong cells, D a misread that would support the conclusion if true. Values checked: 83.3/8.2 = 10.1; 83.3/39.8 = 2.1.

band7.why: Proxy: the graph only bears on the claim through the passage’s GDP ratio (83 times); operations read India, read Nepal, take the ratio, compare with 83; A and C are accurate wrong-cell readings in the key’s frame, D a misreading.

items.subtype: Quotation from a translated verse drama illustrates an indirect claim (reputation owed to circumstance, not character)
items.passage: Mary Stuart is an 1800 play by Friedrich Schiller, translated by Joseph Mellish. In the play, Queen Elizabeth I of England must decide whether to authorize the execution of her cousin and rival, Mary, Queen of Scots. As she deliberates, Elizabeth intimates that her reputation for fairness owes more to her circumstances than to her character: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Mary Stuart most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Have I then practised justice, all my life / Shunned each despotic deed; have I done this / Only to bind my hands against this first, / This necessary act of violence? / My own example now condemns myself!”
“Oh! servitude of popularity! / Disgraceful slavery! How weary am I / Of flattering this idol, which my soul / Despises in its inmost depth! Oh! when / Shall I once more be free upon this throne?”
“I am not made to rule— / A ruler should be made of sterner stuff: / My heart is soft and tender.”

“Had I but been a tyrant, like my sister, / My predecessor, I could fearless then / Have shed this royal blood:—but am I now / Just by my own free choice? No—I was forced / By stern necessity to use this virtue; / Necessity, which binds e’en monarch’s wills.”
items.explanation: The claim is that Elizabeth’s reputation for fairness comes from her situation rather than from her own nature. In choice D she asks whether she is just “by my own free choice” and answers that “stern necessity” forced her to practice that virtue, which says her fairness was imposed by circumstance. That makes D the quotation that illustrates the claim.

A.recipe: LURE/HALF: names her lifelong justice but not its source
A.why_wrong: Elizabeth refers to a lifetime of justice, but she complains that it now ties her hands; she does not say that her fairness was forced on her rather than chosen.

B.recipe: near emotion: resentment of dependence on public favor
B.why_wrong: Elizabeth resents having to court the people’s approval, but the lines say nothing about where her reputation for fairness came from.

C.why_wrong: Here Elizabeth describes her own gentle heart, which would trace her mildness to her character, the opposite of the claim.

sources.what: Schiller, Mary Stuart (1800), Joseph Mellish translation, Project Gutenberg #6791; all four quotations verified verbatim (Act IV, Scenes IX and X; typography normalized to curly quotes and closed em dashes)

items.notes: Band-7 moves: verse drama in translation; claim uses an indirect verb (intimates) and abstract terms (circumstances against character) that the key states only through 'free choice' and 'stern necessity'. Distractors are the same speaker in nearby states: A a lure (practised justice) whose point is constraint, B resentment of popularity, C the opposite stance (her soft heart). Key quotation 45 words (the full sentence); others 20 to 35. B's 'free upon this throne' is a deliberate lure on 'free choice'; it concerns freedom from courting popularity, not the source of her fairness.

band7.why: All four quotations verbatim in Gutenberg #6791 (Act IV, Scenes IX and X). Distractors are good (A justice lure, B near emotion, C opposite stance), but the key says the claim almost outright (“Just by my own free choice? No”, then “I was forced / By stern necessity”) and is the longest option, closer to 3.17 than to 3.37; a lure any nearer the claim would be a second answer, so it stays a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Data completion: condition versus control, the result that runs against the stated expectation
items.passage: Although common bean flowers are capable of fertilizing themselves, bees and other insects that visit them can increase the number of pods and seeds the plants produce. To quantify this contribution on smallholder farms in northern Tanzania, Filemon Elisante and colleagues grew common beans under three treatments: some plants were enclosed in fine mesh that excluded insects, some had their flowers pollinated by hand, and some remained accessible to insect visitors. Because hand pollination supplies each flower with abundant pollen, it is often assumed to produce the highest yield that pollination can achieve. In Elisante and colleagues’ study, however, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: plants left open to insect visitors produced an average of 1,478 kilograms of beans per hectare, more than the 1,131 kilograms per hectare produced by hand-pollinated plants.
hand-pollinated plants produced an average of 1,131 kilograms of beans per hectare, 66 percent more than the plants that were enclosed in mesh to keep insects out.
plants enclosed in mesh to keep insects out produced an average of only 681 kilograms of beans per hectare, less than half as much as plants left open to insects.
plants left open to insect visitors produced 117 percent more beans per hectare than hand-pollinated plants did, an advantage of more than 1,000 kilograms per hectare.

table.title: Average Bean Yield under Three Pollination Treatments
columns: Increase over plants kept from insects (%)

items.explanation: The text says hand pollination is often assumed to produce the highest yield that pollination can achieve, and “however” calls for a result that runs against that assumption. The table shows that plants left open to insects averaged 1,478 kilograms per hectare, more than the 1,131 kilograms of hand-pollinated plants. Choice A reports that result, so it completes the statement.

B.recipe: IRREL: accurate but consistent with the assumption
B.why_wrong: This is accurate, but hand-pollinated plants outyielding plants kept from insects is just what the assumption about hand pollination predicts, so it does not contrast with it.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate, not about the assumption
C.why_wrong: This is accurate and shows that insects matter, as the text’s first sentence says they can, but it compares open plants with plants kept from insects, not with hand-pollinated plants, so it says nothing against the assumption.

D.recipe: INACC: misplaced value (percentage belongs to a different comparison)
D.why_wrong: The 117 percent in the table is the gain of open plants over plants kept from insects, not over hand-pollinated plants; open plants outyielded hand-pollinated plants by only about 350 kilograms per hectare.

sources.what: Elisante et al. 2020, PeerJ 8: e10102, 'Insect pollination is important in a smallholder bean farming system' (Arusha region, Tanzania; Kariasii common bean): Table 1 average yield per hectare open 1,478 kg (117% over self), hand 1,131 kg (66%), self (bagged with polyethylene net to exclude pollinators) 681 kg; common bean is autogamous

items.notes: Band-7 moves (Q1_P5 surprise, after 3.38): the passage gives only the assumption (hand pollination yields the most) and “however”, so the student must work out which result runs against it; two distractors are accurate results that fit the assumption, one misplaces the table’s percentage. The first sentence states that insects can raise yields so that C is not itself a surprise. Options 27 to 29 words. Values checked: 1,478 > 1,131; 681/1,478 = 0.46; 1,131/681 = 1.66.

fixes: passage: expectation no longer spelled out (“so plants accessible to insects would be expected to yield no more than hand-pollinated plants. Contrary to that expectation”); now the assumption plus “however”, so the student must find the result that contradicts it (hardening); explanation and B, C reasons updated

band7.why: After the fix: passage 100 words, Q1 options 27 to 29 words, the surprise must be inferred from the hand-pollination assumption as in 3.38; B and C are accurate readings that fit the assumption, D misplaces the 117 percent.

items.subtype: Data description: condition versus control with extra conditions (free glasses alone against free glasses with upgrade offers)
items.passage: Programs that distribute free eyeglasses to schoolchildren can improve the children’s vision and academic performance, but such programs may also reduce sales of glasses, an important source of revenue for many eye-care providers, since families who receive a complimentary pair have little reason to purchase one. In a trial at rural primary schools in China’s Guangdong and Yunnan provinces, Nathan Congdon and colleagues gave some children who needed glasses a prescription only, gave others free glasses, and gave two additional groups free glasses along with an offer to purchase more fashionable “upgrade” glasses for $15 or $30. The researchers concluded that offering upgrade glasses can prevent free-glasses programs from reducing sales.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: In each of the four groups, the families of fewer than 25 percent of the children bought glasses during the trial, though the percentages differed somewhat from group to group.
The families of about 13 percent of the children who received free glasses bought glasses, roughly half the percentage in the prescription-only group.
Purchases in both groups offered upgrade glasses nearly matched those in the prescription-only group, while purchases in the group given only free glasses were much lower.
Families of children who were offered $30 upgrade glasses bought glasses about twice as often as families of children who received a prescription only.

figure.title: Children Whose Families Bought Glasses, by Trial Group
figure.description: Four bars; y-axis 0 to 30 in steps of 5. Prescription only about 24%; free glasses about 13%; free glasses plus $15 upgrade offer about 21%; free glasses plus $30 upgrade offer about 21%.

items.explanation: The researchers conclude that adding an upgrade offer keeps free glasses from cutting into sales. That requires two things: free glasses alone lower purchases compared with a prescription only, and purchases in the upgrade groups stay near the prescription-only level. The graph shows about 13 percent for free glasses alone against about 24 percent for prescription only, and about 21 percent in each upgrade group. Choice C describes that whole pattern.

A.recipe: IRREL: true of every group
A.why_wrong: This is accurate, but a low rate in every group does not show that the upgrade offers made any difference.

B.recipe: PART: half the comparison
B.why_wrong: This shows only that free glasses reduced purchases; it leaves out the upgrade groups, so it cannot show that the offers prevented the drop.

D.why_wrong: The $30 upgrade group’s rate, about 21 percent, was slightly lower than the prescription-only group’s, about 24 percent, not twice as high.

sources.what: Wang X, Congdon N, et al. 2017, PLoS ONE 12(11): e0187808, PRICE (Potentiating Rural Investment in Children's Eyecare) cluster-randomized trial, Guangdong and Yunnan: glasses purchase control 23.6%, free glasses 12.7%, free + $15 upgrade 21.3%, free + $30 upgrade 20.9%; upgrade glasses prevented the reduction in purchases

items.notes: Band 6 (condition versus control with a design wrinkle, two added conditions). The key needs all three levels; B is the partial reading, A true of every group, D a false reading. The near-equal $15 and $30 bars are never compared in an option.

band7.why: Target 6 met: a design wrinkle (two upgrade arms), the key needs all three levels; A true of every group, B the partial reading, D false.

items.subtype: Data completion: pairwise comparison holding one variable fixed (same wind speed, colder air)
items.passage: Wind makes cold air feel colder because it continually strips away the thin layer of warmed air that insulates exposed skin. The US National Weather Service quantifies this effect with a wind chill index, a “feels like” temperature calculated from the air temperature and the wind speed using a model of heat loss from the human face that was tested on volunteers. According to the index, a given wind lowers the perceived temperature more dramatically when the air is already extremely cold than when it is relatively mild. For example, whereas a 20-mile-per-hour wind makes air at 30°F feel like 17°F, a drop of 13 degrees, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: a 40-mile-per-hour wind makes air at 30°F feel like 13°F, a drop of 17 degrees.
the same wind makes air at 10°F feel like −4°F, a drop of 14 degrees.
a 40-mile-per-hour wind makes air at −10°F feel like −43°F, a drop of 33 degrees.
the same wind makes air at −10°F feel like −35°F, a drop of 25 degrees.

table.title: Wind Chill (°F) at Selected Air Temperatures and Wind Speeds

items.explanation: The example must keep the wind the same, 20 miles per hour, and show a bigger drop at a colder air temperature. The table shows that a 20-mile-per-hour wind makes air at −10°F feel like −35°F, a drop of 25 degrees, which is larger than the 13-degree drop at 30°F. Choice D completes the example.

A.recipe: TRAP: wrong variable changed (temperature fixed, wind changed)
A.why_wrong: This keeps the air at 30°F and changes the wind speed, so it says nothing about how the same wind acts on colder air.

B.recipe: INACC: value from the wrong row
B.why_wrong: In the table, −4°F is the wind chill for a 10-mile-per-hour wind at 10°F; a 20-mile-per-hour wind makes 10°F feel like −9°F.

C.recipe: TRAP: two variables changed at once
C.why_wrong: Both the wind speed and the temperature differ from the 30°F example, so the larger drop cannot be credited to the colder air alone.

sources.what: US National Weather Service wind chill chart and formula, WC = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75V^0.16 + 0.4275TV^0.16 (based on a human face model, tested on 12 subjects); table values computed with the formula and rounded as on the NWS chart (page example: 0 F with 15 mph gives -19 F)

items.notes: Plan lists this cell as band 7, but spec/rw/band7/command_of_evidence.md says Q1_P3 has no band-7 official items ('do not aim them at band 7'), so it is written as a strong band 6 per WAVE.md. Like 3.29, the key fixes one variable and changes the other; A and C change the wrong variable or both, B lifts the 10-mph value. Values checked with the NWS formula: 20 mph at 30 F = 17, at 10 F = -9, at -10 F = -35; 40 mph at 30 F = 13, at -10 F = -43; 10 mph at 10 F = -4.

band7.why: Q1_P3 has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6 as written: the key holds the wind fixed while A and C change it and B lifts the 10-mph value. All 12 cells match the NWS formula.

items.subtype: Data completion: extreme after a filter the passage sets (tallest dam of the two types that need no narrow gorge)
items.passage: Most of the world’s tallest dams belong to one of three structural types. Arch dams curve upstream so that the water’s pressure is transferred into the walls of the canyon, which allows them to hold back deep reservoirs with considerably less concrete. Because an arch dam depends on solid rock on both sides, engineers can build one only in a narrow gorge with strong walls. Gravity dams, which resist the water’s force through their sheer weight, and embankment dams, which are massive mounds of compacted earth or rock, face no such restriction. Among the dams in the table, the tallest dam of these two types is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: the Grande Dixence Dam in Switzerland, which is 285 meters tall.
the Nurek Dam in Tajikistan, which is 300 meters tall.
the Jinping-I Dam in China, which is 305 meters tall.
the Xiaowan Dam in China, which is 292 meters tall.

table.title: Five of the World’s Tallest Dams

items.explanation: The text says gravity and embankment dams face no such restriction, so the blank asks for the tallest dam of those two types. The table lists two: Nurek, an embankment dam 300 meters tall, and Grande Dixence, a gravity dam 285 meters tall. Nurek is the taller, so choice B completes the statement.

A.recipe: right type, wrong extreme
A.why_wrong: Grande Dixence is a gravity dam, so it is one of the two types, but at 285 meters it is shorter than the 300-meter Nurek Dam, an embankment dam.

C.recipe: WGRP: tallest overall but the wrong type
C.why_wrong: Jinping-I is the tallest dam in the table, but it is an arch dam, the type the text says can be built only in a narrow gorge, not a gravity or embankment dam.

D.why_wrong: Xiaowan is an arch dam, so it is not one of the two types the statement refers to, and it is shorter than the Jinping-I Dam in any case.

sources.what: Wikipedia, List of tallest dams: Jinping-I 305 m concrete arch China; Nurek 300 m embankment (earth-fill) Tajikistan; Xiaowan 292 m concrete arch China; Grande Dixence 285 m concrete gravity Switzerland; Enguri 271.5 m concrete arch Georgia

items.notes: Band 7 (Q1_P2 with a filter, after 3.44): the filter is set by the passage (gravity or embankment, the types with no gorge restriction), then the extreme. A is the right type at the wrong extreme, C the tallest row of the wrong type (the 3.44 trap), D another wrong-type row. Value-only options as in the model. Reviewer rebuilt it on height and dropped the year column, since Enguri’s completion year is given as 1978 or 1987 by different sources. Nurek is sometimes given as 304 m; either figure leaves it taller than Grande Dixence and the key unchanged.

fixes: rebuilt on height so nothing depends on Enguri’s completion year (1978 on the list, 1987 elsewhere): year column dropped, the blank now asks for the tallest dam of the two types the passage says need no narrow gorge (gravity, embankment); key moved from Enguri to Nurek, still B; options, explanation, distractors and notes rewritten

band7.why: One filter then an extreme, as in 3.44 (the only band-7 Q1_P2 item), with the filter set by a passage relation rather than named in the blank; C is the tallest row of the wrong type, A the right type at the wrong extreme. Value-only options follow 3.44.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a group-comparison hypothesis (effect largest for one subgroup)
items.passage: Although Kenya abolished tuition fees in public primary schools in 2003, most schools still require uniforms, which can cost a poor family a substantial share of its income. A child without a uniform may also feel embarrassed among classmates who have one. Economists David Evans, Michael Kremer, and Mũthoni Ngatia gave free uniforms to randomly chosen pupils in western Kenya and then monitored how frequently those pupils and their classmates were absent. The researchers hypothesized that a free uniform would reduce absenteeism, especially among children who had never owned one.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ hypothesis?
options: Students who received a free uniform missed fewer days of school than students who did not, especially if they had owned no uniform before the study.
Among students who did not receive a free uniform, those who already owned a uniform missed about as many days of school as those who did not own one.
Students who received a free uniform scored higher on end-of-year examinations than did students in the same schools who were not selected to receive one.
Parents of students who received a free uniform reported spending less money on clothing that year than parents of the other students did.
items.explanation: The researchers predicted that a free uniform would cut absences, and cut them most for students who had never owned a uniform. Choice A reports fewer absences among students who received uniforms than among those who did not, with the largest difference for students who had owned none, which is exactly the pattern the hypothesis predicts.

B.recipe: wrong comparison (within the untreated group), points away
B.why_wrong: This compares students who never received a free uniform, and it suggests owning a uniform made little difference to absences, which does not support the hypothesis.

C.why_wrong: Higher exam scores do not show that the uniforms reduced absences, let alone that they did so most for students who had owned none.

D.why_wrong: Lower clothing costs for families say nothing about whether students missed fewer days of school.

sources.what: Evans, Kremer and Ngatia, randomized distribution of free school uniforms in western Kenya (Busia); providing a uniform reduced absenteeism, with the largest effect for children who had no uniform before (IPA summary; Evans and Ngatia 2018 World Bank WPS8421 reports 37% overall and 55% for those without a prior uniform)

items.notes: Medium: the claim is comparative and moderated, so the key needs the treated-versus-untreated comparison plus the subgroup. B compares within the control group, C and D are off-target outcomes. The key matches the study's real result.

fixes: passage: stigma motive no longer attributed to the named economists (the IPA summary does not give it); now a general sentence
medium density: plainer words

items.subtype: Quotation from a novel illustrates a two-part claim (provoked by students, yet keeps his self-control)
items.passage: The Hoosier Schoolmaster is an 1871 novel by Edward Eggleston. In the novel, Ralph Hartsook, a young man from a small Indiana town, takes a job as schoolmaster in the backwoods settlement of Flat Creek, where unruly older students have intimidated and driven away previous instructors. Eggleston suggests that Ralph maintains his self-control in front of his students even when they deliberately provoke him: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from The Hoosier Schoolmaster most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “Hartsook’s first day was hurried and unsatisfactory. He was not of himself, and consequently not master of anybody else.”
“He ate with deliberation, and looked everybody in the eyes with a manner that made Bud watch him curiously.”
“Ralph Hartsook grew red in the face when he saw the puppy. But the cool, repressed, bulldog mood in which he had kept himself saved him.”
“When evening came, there were symptoms of insubordination through the whole school. Poor Ralph was sick at heart.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Ralph’s students provoke him, and he still keeps his self-control in front of them. In choice C, Ralph grows “red in the face” at the puppy his students have hidden, yet the “cool, repressed, bulldog mood” he has kept up “saved him.” Only C shows both the provocation and Ralph holding on to his self-control.

A.recipe: OPP: loses self-control
A.why_wrong: Here Ralph is “not of himself” and not in control of anyone, which shows him losing his self-control rather than keeping it.

B.recipe: HALF: self-control without provocation
B.why_wrong: Ralph behaves deliberately at breakfast, but nothing provokes him and his students are not present, so only one part of the claim is shown.

D.recipe: HALF: provocation and distress without self-control
D.why_wrong: The students’ unruliness provokes Ralph, but the quotation shows only that he is unhappy, not that he keeps his self-control in front of them.

sources.what: Edward Eggleston, The Hoosier School-Master (1871), Project Gutenberg #15099, Chapter I; all four quotations verified verbatim

items.notes: Medium two-part claim (provoked, yet keeps his self-control). B and D are half-matches (self-control without provocation; provocation without self-control), A the opposite, as in the medium literary models. The claim says self-control rather than outward composure because the key's Ralph visibly reddens.

fixes: medium density: “village” to “town”, “keeps” to “maintains”

items.subtype: Quotation from a novel illustrates a contrast claim (usual expression against a livelier side seen only at times)
items.passage: Esther Waters is an 1894 novel by George Moore. The novel opens as Esther, a twenty-year-old woman from an impoverished London family, arrives by train to begin employment as a kitchen maid at a wealthy family’s countryside estate. In characterizing Esther, Moore indicates that her usual demeanor conceals a livelier disposition that emerges only occasionally: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from Esther Waters most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “The nose was too thick, but the nostrils were well formed. The eyes were grey, luminous, and veiled with dark lashes.”
“But it was only when she laughed that her face lost its habitual expression, which was somewhat sullen; then it flowed with bright humour.”
“She smiled, and her face became as bright as the month: it was the first day of June.”
“The girl gazed on this bleak country like one who saw it for the first time. She saw without perceiving, for her mind was occupied with personal consideration.”
items.explanation: The claim contrasts Esther’s usual expression with a livelier side that appears only at times. Choice B gives both parts: her “habitual expression” is “somewhat sullen,” and “only when she laughed” does her face fill “with bright humour.” The other quotations show either her features or a single bright moment, not the contrast.

A.recipe: OFF: physical features, no change of expression
A.why_wrong: This lists Esther’s features, some plain and some attractive, but says nothing about her usual expression giving way to a livelier one.

C.recipe: HALF: the bright moment without the usual expression
C.why_wrong: Esther’s face brightens here, but nothing indicates that her ordinary look hides this side of her, so only half the contrast is shown.

D.why_wrong: The bleakness belongs to the countryside, and the lines describe Esther’s preoccupation, not an expression that gives way to liveliness.

sources.what: George Moore, Esther Waters (1894), Project Gutenberg #8157, Chapter I; all four quotations verified verbatim

items.notes: Medium contrast claim; the key alone has both halves (usual sullen look, brightness when she laughs). C is the half-match, A off-target, D a lure on 'bleak'.

fixes: medium density: “ordinary” to “usual”, “suggests” to “indicates”

items.subtype: Data completion: comparison of two measures that illustrates a stated pattern
items.passage: Many households in sub-Saharan Africa got phone service from mobile networks without ever being connected to the fixed telephone lines that once carried nearly all calls, a pattern that economists call “leapfrogging.” Because running copper wire to widely dispersed rural homes is expensive, mobile networks could reach people much more quickly and cheaply. Leapfrogging is particularly evident in World Bank data from 2010: for example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
